David Olds  

The second issue of volume 27 of Neuropsychoanalysis features a target article by William Singletary and Timothy Rice entitled “Two Diverging Paths in Psychological and Neurobiological Organization: Using or Refusing Love” (Singletary & Rice, 2025). The authors examine the impact of adverse childhood experiences and the child’s role in coping with their consequences. They contrast open-system functioning, characterized by basic trust and secure attachment, with closed-system functioning, defined by the rejection of love when it becomes available. The article emphasizes the mechanisms through which persistent stress responses contribute to maladaptive developmental trajectories, often resulting in chronic feelings of loneliness that compromise both mental and physical health. Singletary and Rice review psychological and neurobiological research to describe the two diverging pathways. They highlight the significance of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis as well as a hypothesis of the interactions between the oxytocin and the vasopressin systems. Additionally, the authors review the effects of adverse childhood experiences on different brain regions including the amygdala, insula, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex. Brief case vignettes illustrate instances of closed-system functioning. The paper concludes with a discussion on therapeutic approaches aimed at facilitating the transition from closed-system functioning to open-system functioning in children who reject available love.

This comprehensive target article is followed by commentaries from several authors whose work relates to the topic of the paper. The initial commentary was authored by Gregory Rizzolo, who praises the inclusion of neurobiological literature to explore a long-standing issue within psychoanalytic theories. Rizzolo (2025) questions whether closed – and open-system functioning should be conceptualized as points along a continuum of openness and closedness rather than as extreme categories. He also questions the extent to which the child plays an active role in the refusal of love. In his commentary, Leon Hoffman discusses the complexities of development and agrees with Rizzolo regarding the value of an integrative approach encompassing both psychological and neurobiological dimensions of maladaptive development. Hoffman (2025) clarifies Singletary and Rice’s idea that children who experienced early trauma may be unable to overcome the defense mechanisms that once protected them against adverse situations. Hoffman concludes by considering the implications of closed-system functioning and the potential evolutionary role of aggression.

Two Diverging Paths in Psychological and Neurobiological Organization: Using or Refusing Love

William Singletary and Timothy Rice

Timothy Rice

Philadelphia, PA, USA
wsingletarymd@gmail.com

New York, NY, USA

New York, NY, USA

Timothy Rice  

Development, early adversity, neuropsychoanalysis, neurobiology, loneliness, emotion regulation

Difficulties in early development, such as adverse childhood experiences, interfere with the formation of social connections and lead to deleterious outcomes in emotional and physical health across the lifespan. While a child’s actual experiences with parents are well-known to be significant, less well appreciated is the child’s role in shaping developmental outcomes. Some children may form defensive and ultimately maladaptive structures and actively refuse available love and support. This manuscript develops an integrative neuropsychoanalytic model based on evolutionary and complex dynamic systems theories involving the psychological, neurobiological, as well as general biological processes and pathways which lead to either secure attachment, loving object constancy, and health, or to insecure attachment, hostile object constancy, and illness. Positive outcomes represent open-system functioning that involves using love, promoting optimal plasticity. Negative outcomes represent the opposite: closed-system functioning where the child refuses available love and becomes stuck in a world of mistrust, stress, and adversity. Effective prevention and treatment of closed-system functioning promote biological and psychological plasticity and help patients become open to experiencing positive relationships and promote lifelong health and wellbeing.

Aggression and Conflict and Compromise Formation: Discussion of “Two Diverging Paths in Psychological and Neurobiological Organization: Using or Refusing Love” by William Singletary and Timothy Rice

Leon Hoffman

Leon Hoffman

USA
NYPI 167 East 67th Street, New York, NY 10065
hoffman.leon@gmail.com

Leon Hoffman  

ARTICLE HISTORY Received 30 September 2025; Accepted 10 November 2025

In their essay, “Two diverging paths in psychological and neurobiological organization: Using or refusing love,” William Singletary and Timothy Rice provide us with a very rich work in which they integrate neuroscience findings with psychological findings, particularly those which are derived from psychoanalytic ideas.

They summarize their thesis noting that “early life experiences of actual danger or perceived danger,” (Singletary & Rice, 2025, p. 10). that is, situations which promote a great deal of ongoing stress to the developing infant, lead to “epigenetic changes in the oxytocin/vasopressin system with maladaptive consequences over a lifetime.” (p. 10). Oxytocin facilitates cooperative human connectedness and vasopressin promotes aggression, vigilance, and defensive behavior. As a result of the stress there is an allostatic load, that is, a cumulative effect on the body of the chronic exposure to the stressful stimuli. This leads to both physiological and psychological damage. This allostatic load prevents the establishment of stable homeostasis, both physically and psychologically. As a result there are two paths to development: one in which safety and metabolizing love is predominant and the second, refusing love and experiencing loneliness and illness.

An important clinical example describes this second, pathological, outcome: a view of the world as an unsafe place. They describe a young boy who left a toy in Dr. Singletary’s office. “Before he came to the next session, I placed this toy on a table for him. When he walked into my office, he saw his toy and immediately exclaimed, ‘You stole my toy!’” (Singletary & Rice, 2025, p. 5). In a very simple way, this example illustrates how a little boy, undoubtedly traumatized and in a constant state of stress, refuses to or cannot accept the love provided by the adult through returning his toy.

Evolution of the Vicissitudes of Aggression

This contribution by Singletary and Rice provides a great deal of material to help us understand the relationship between basic physiological and neurological activities and the power of social connections and love in the promotion of healthy development. But a question remains.

A Commentary On: “Two Diverging Paths in Psychological and Neurobiological Organization: Using or Refusing Love” by William Singletary and Timothy Rice

Thomas Barrett

Thomas Barrett

30 North Michigan Ave. #1300, Chicago, IL 60602, US
tfbarrettphd@gmail.com

Thomas Barrett  

Development, attachment, object constancy, loneliness, “metabolizing” love

In this commentary I review this important and timely contribution. Noted is its consideration of many perspectives and disciplines as they formulate and articulate a “Two Path” developmental model that contrasts the consequences of living and growing in an environment that offers safety, security, and predictability, vs one that is fraught with danger, insecurity and unpredictability. They importantly note the influences of the hormonal contributions of oxytocin and vasopressin, and their respective ratios, as they appear in the contrasting development of persons on the differing paths. Also admired is the authors’ recognition and acknowledgment of the now more broadly recognized influence of loneliness. They note its contribution to both mental and physical health and well-being. Their theory building concludes with review of the pathway to the attainment of the developmental accomplishment of mastering an integrated and available sense of object constancy, an essential process in achieving the reliably available ability to “metabolize love,” that is to receive, use, and return love, rather than refusing it. This commentary concludes with the mention of noteworthy programs and resources in the literature that support programs of primary prevention, early intervention, and/or psychotherapy/psychoanalysis.

Gerald Wiest  

Functional disorder, neurology, bayesian, predictive, coding

In his article “‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders: The Common Ground of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis,” Mark Solms offers a look back at the beginnings of psychoanalysis through to the current neuropsychoanalytical concepts of somatoform disorders. He spans the arc from Freud's first work on the genesis of hysteria and conversion neuroses and his early models of the psychic apparatus – which were still very much based on the neurological reflex arc model – to current neuroscientific findings that neuropsychoanalysis seeks to link with metapsychology. This specific starting point of neuropsychoanalysis, the so-called dual-aspect monism, postulates that mind and body consist of the same “material,” but are viewed from two different perspectives. This neurophilosophical view makes it possible to understand mental and physical phenomena as two aspects of a single underlying reality. The application of the neuroscientific concept of “predictive coding” with regard to the development of functional neurological disorders represents one of the most innovative and now widely accepted approaches in neuro-psychosomatics [Hallett, M., Aybek, S., Ceranic, B., Czarnecki, K., Daum, C., Edwards, M. J., Espay, A. J., Fung, V. S. C., Ganos, C., Guerreiro, R., Hinson, V. K., Kanaan, R., Kranick, S. M., LaFaver, K., Lang, A. E., Lehn, A., Lidstone, S. C., Maurer, C. W., Mildon, B.,…Voon, V. (2022). Functional neurological disorder: New subtypes and shared mechanisms. The Lancet Neurology, 21(6), 537–550. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(21)00422-1] and shows us how our perception is not only the sum of our sensory impressions, but is also strongly influenced by our expectations.

Igor Grujičić Philosopher and interactive psychotherapist, graduated in Philosophy from the Faculty of Philosophy in Novi Sad. He serves as a senior associate at the Institute for Philosophy and Interdisciplinary Studies in Novi Sad, where he conducts his in-depth research on various philosophical and psychoanalytic topics, as well as in psychotherapeutic practice. As the founder of the academic association “The Soul House,” Igor is dedicated to educating the public about philosophical and psychological sciences, promoting knowledge and facilitating the exchange of ideas in these fields. He is also the editor of the journal Agrafa, a publication focused on the philosophy of psychoanalysis, which enhances the dissemination of valuable academic knowledge through the publication of relevant papers. His work employs an interdisciplinary approach that combines philosophy and psychotherapy to deepen understanding of the human psyche and emotional processes while developing theoretical frameworks for interactive psychoanalysis. Mark Fisher Professor of Neurology at UC Irvine. He has appointments in the UCI Departments of Anatomy & Neurobiology, Pathology & Laboratory Medicine, and Political Science and is Director of the UCI Center for Neuropolitics. He has received more than 50 citations of clinical excellence from external organizations for his work as a stroke neurologist and his stroke research has been funded by the NIH for the past 40 years. He is a member of the American Psychoanalytic Association and directs the Discussion Group Neuroscience Perspectives on Psychoanalysis. Maria Sonia Goergen Pediatric neurologist and the coordinator of neuroplaybrasil.com. Sara Uccella Child neuropsychiatrist and psychotherapist with special training in early childhood development and sleep physiology. She is working on a research project on prematurity and mental development. She collaborates with the Department of Neonatology and Child Neuropsychiatry at the Giannina Gaslini Hospital in Genoa and the Hopital CHU Lenval in Nice to develop care pathways for families of neurologically vulnerable infants and children and adolescents with neurological (including rare) and psychiatric conditions. She has studied and worked in several European and non-European cities exploring the relationship between mind and body. She has published in international scientific journals. Eric Sanford Third-year psychiatry resident in the physician scientist track at Mount Sinai Hospital. He previously studied neuroscience at Brown University (completing an Honors thesis in Thomas Serre's lab). He then worked in computational biology group at Foundation Medicine, where he co-authored several publications in cancer genomics under the mentorship of Siraj Ali, Garrett Frampton, and James Sun. He received his MD and PhD in Genomics and Computational Biology from the University of Pennsylvania. His dissertation, completed in Arjun Raj's systems biology lab, combined molecular biology, mathematical modeling, and genomics methods to characterize how genes combine the transcriptional effects of interacting input signals. He found that gene regulation appeared to have a preference for the operations of either addition or multiplication when combining the effects of two cell signals. His current research now focuses on how the brain combines the effects of multiple primary affective systems. Andreas Lehrner Vienna, is a caretaker for mentally ill persons. He regards neuropsychoanalytic thinking, and especially the concept of the seven emotional drives, as immensely useful for that work. He is a candidate at the WAP (Wiener Arbeitskreis für Psychoanalyse) and organizes webinars with Mark Solms for WPA (Wiener Psychoanalytische Akademie). Karam Radwan Currently serves as Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, Section Chief of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, and Director of the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Fellowship Program at the University of Chicago. Since 2008, Dr. Radwan has co-taught, alongside Dr. Kellman, a course on psychodynamic therapy for child psychiatry fellows. This longstanding course emphasizes psychodynamic principles, developmental psychopathology, and therapeutic interventions tailored specifically for children and adolescents. Kristin Rosseau Board-certified Adult and Child and Adolescent psychiatrist. She is an assistant professor within the Psychiatry Department at University Of Chicago. Dr. Rosseau's areas of interest are psychodynamic and psychoanalytic psychotherapy, physician wellness, medical student education, and selective mutism. Vijay Khilanani Child, Adolescent & Adult Psychiatrist, Addiction Medicine Specialist, and a Psychoanalyst. He practices in a partial hospital program in Chicago, while simultaneously maintaining his private practice. Joshua Kellman Child and adult psychiatrist and a psychoanalyst. He is on the faculty at the University of Chicago, in the department of psychiatry, predominantly in the section of child and adolescent psychiatry. He teaches classes on psychodynamic work with children and adults, and on development. He is also involved in research on play, including a recent study involving parents tickling their children, examining the relationship between heart rate variability and play, and the relationship between play and flexibility. He is also on the faculty at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, where he teaches classes on psychoanalysis and neuroscience, on the hierarchical models approach to psychoanalysis, and case conferences. He also has a private practice in Wilmette, Illinois. Andrei Novac Clinical professor of psychiatry at the University of California, Irvine and a clinical associate at the New Center for Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles. Dr. Novac was born in Bucharest, Romania and is the son of Holocaust survivors. He immigrated in his 20s to the United States. After medical school, he trained first in pediatrics, and then completed a residency and fellowship in psychiatry at the University of California, Irvine. He later held the position of Founding Director of the Traumatic Stress Program at UC, Irvine. Dr. Novac has been a practicing psychiatrist, psychotherapist, and more recently, psychoanalyst. His main subjects of expertise are: Intergenerational transmission of trauma; neuropsychoanalysis; free association; identity narrative and autobiographical memory; and emotional synchrony. He is the author of over 50 scientific papers in peer review journals and book chapters and has lectured on these topics internationally. He has also published four books of poetry. Pól Ó'Mórdha Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychiatry, School of Medicine, Trinity College Dublin and Course Director of the M.Sc. in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. Pól is a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, in private practice in Dublin and Carlow, Ireland. He is also a visiting faculty member of the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis (NPAP) in New York. Pól is a former Chair of the Irish Institute of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (IIPP), and is also a Training Analyst with the IIPP. He is also an associate editor for the journal Neuropsychoanalysis. Pól is co-leader, with Barbara Fitzgerald, of the Neuropsychoanalysis Ireland Study Group. He collaborates with Professor Oliver Turnbull’s Emotion Research Lab at Bangor University North Wales, where the team are investigating the neural correlates of psychotherapy – in this context Pól has worked psychoanalytically, both long-term and short-term, with people who have profound amnesia as a consequence of a brain injury. Marcel G.J. Schmeets (Child) psychiatrist/psychoanalyst, former head of Child and Adolescent Department of the Dutch Psychoanalytic Institute in Amsterdam/Utrecht, now working in private practice. He was co-founder, and first chair of board, of the Dutch Association for Infant Mental Health (DAIMH), and chair of the local organizing committee 16th Annual Congress NPSA in Amsterdam 2015. He is a former chair a.i. and former secretary of the Training Committee of the Dutch Psychoanalytic Society. Selin Sert Yurdakul Medical doctor and internal medicine specialist, currently pursuing a Ph.D. in Neuroscience at Bahçeşehir University. She is the director of the Palliative Care Unit at Kanuni Sultan Süleyman Training and Research Hospital, where she also supervises medical residents working with a multidisciplinary approach. Her research focuses on the interplay between stress, chronic illness, and autonomic nervous system functioning. A member of the Society for the Exploration of Psychotherapy Integration (SEPI), Dr. Yurdakul is committed to bridging psychoanalytic and body-oriented therapies within an integrative framework. Her clinical work and research explore how early developmental trauma and implicit emotional memory are embodied and processed through autonomic nervous system regulation. She continues advanced training in neuropsychoanalysis through clinical seminars with Mark Solms and Dr. Andrea Clarici. Hana Kodba-Čeh Clinical psychology resident with training in developmental analytical psychotherapy and a researcher at the Golnik University Clinic. She is also a doctoral candidate at the Department of Psychology, Faculty of Arts, University of Ljubljana, where her research focuses on the developmental aspects of the dying process. She previously worked as a researcher on the ACTION project, conducted across six European countries, studying an advance care planning intervention for cancer patients. She later led a large-scale, multi-site qualitative study on the iLIVE project, which examined end-of-life experiences in 13 countries. In her role as a psychologist, she conducts assessments and provides individual counseling, therapy, and group supervision for healthcare professionals. Yuli Fradkin I conducted both clinical research and provided clinical care to children and adolescents with autism and language impairment as a Child and Adolescent psychiatrist attending at Rutgers University Behavioral Health Clinic and a faculty member at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School research has focused broadly on the underlying neurophysiology, neuropathology and genetics of neuropsychiatric disorders. As a Child and Adolescent Psychiatrist, I have a specific interest in the underlying neurodevelopmental pathology contributing to childhood onset disorders such as autism spectrum disorder, mood disorders and language impairment. The proposed study will address one of the most difficult challenges in child and adolescent psychiatry, reliably diagnosing psychosis in children. Language disturbances associated with psychosis would be investigated as predictors and characteristics of illness progression. Ana Delgadillo Holds a degree in psychology and a Master’s degree in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. She is currently conducting doctoral research in psychoanalysis with a focus on neuropsychoanalysis at the Universidad Intercontinental. She has a specialty in polygraphy from the CISEN (National Institute of Statistics and Censuses). She worked for the Mexico City Government in the Ministry of Citizen Security, the General Attorney Office, and the Comptroller General Office. She teaches courses related to criminal profiling and psychopathology at the Center for Advanced Studies in Criminology. She is an assistant lecturer of Psychosomatics in the Master’s program in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy at the Universidad Intercontinental. Adam Omary Ph.D. student in Psychology at Harvard University. He received his B.A. in Cognitive Science and M.S. in Biostatistics from the University of Southern California. His research focuses on how sex hormones influence brain development and give rise to psychological sex differences. He aims to provide a mechanistic account of psychosexual development, synthesizing evidence from psychoanalytic theory, behavioral endocrinology, and developmental neuroscience. Inna Rosentsvit Neurologist, neurorehabilitation and neurodiversity specialist, and psychoanalytically trained clinician whose work bridges neuroscience, psychoanalysis, and psychohistory. She is the founder and Executive Director of Neurorecovery Solutions, a nonprofit supporting neurodiverse individuals and their families through education, advocacy, and neuro-coaching. Her clinical and research focus includes neuroplasticity, psychosocial development, parent–child dynamics, and the transgenerational transmission of trauma and resilience. Dr. Rozentsvit serves as the Programs Director at the Object Relations Institute for Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, where she teaches courses on neuropsychoanalysis, psychosomatics, and transdisciplinary approaches to mental health. She is also Associate Director of the Psychohistory Forum, Co-Leader of its Psychobiography Research and Publication Group, and Associate Editor of Clio’s Psyche. Her work draws on foundational neurobiological concepts, Eric Kandel’s principles of mental functioning, Paul MacLean’s Triune Brain model, and her own Functional Psychoneurobiology Tools®, to understand how early developmental experiences shape neural architecture and long-term psychological functioning. She has written and presented widely on how therapeutic relationships, empathy, and mindful practices can rewire the brain’s maladaptive circuits through self-directed neuroplasticity. In her psychohistorical writing, she explores how early neurodevelopmental dynamics shape not only individual lives but also cultural narratives, identity formation, and collective behavior. Dr. Rozentsvit’s work exemplifies a deeply integrative framework for healing, bridging science, clinical insight, and historical awareness to support more adaptive futures. Victoria Grinman Psychotherapist, educator, speaker, and mentor to clinicians, specializing in post-traumatic growth, relational wellness, and trauma integration. With nearly two decades of experience supporting individuals and families across life stages, she is known for her integrative, human-centered approach to healing and transformation. Dr. Grinman is the author of a chapter in The Routledge International Handbook of Posttraumatic Growth, where she explores the lived experiences and perceptions of PTG in parents of young adults diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Her clinical work and research focus on the long-view journey of growth after adversity – one that honors meaning-making, cultural context, and the neuroplastic potential of the human brain. She is passionate about helping clinicians recognize PTG as a lens for practice that transcends modality and deepens therapeutic presence. Jeffrey Rubin Psychoanalyst, psychotherapist, teacher, author, and psychobiographer. He practices psychoanalysis and psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy in New York City and North Salem, NY. Dr. Rubin teaches at the Object Relations Institute, the American Institute for Psychoanalysis, and the C. G. Jung Institute of New York. He has taught and lectured widely at psychoanalytic institutes, meditation and yoga centers, and academic institutions in the U.S. and abroad. He is the author of eight books, including A Psychoanalysis for Our Time, The Good Life, Psychotherapy and Buddhism, The Art of Flourishing, Meditative Psychotherapy, and Practicing Meditative Psychotherapy, with two forthcoming works: Psychotherapy Case Studies: Escaping the Prison You Didn’t Know You Were In, and Meditative Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis: Pathways to Healing and Transformation. His work on integrating Eastern and Western healing traditions, particularly psychoanalysis, Buddhism, and meditation, has been described as pioneering. His approach to therapy was featured in The New York Times Magazine under the term “Enlightenment Therapy.” Dr. Rubin advocates for a pluralistic and integrative psychoanalysis that values insight across traditions and disciplines, including history, literature, art, and anthropology, to deepen our understanding of the human condition. More information: www.drjeffreyrubin.com. Alexey Tolchinsky Clinical psychologist in private practice in Maryland, U.S.A. He is a Clinical Fellow of NPSA. His research interest includes the application of non-linear dynamical systems to the theories of consciousness and psychopathology, as well as active inference, narrative fallacy, trauma, dissociative experiences, and OCD. A common theme in these papers is a highlight of how the natural limitations of our theoretical models influence clinical practice. For example, a historical bias toward determinism in psychiatry and clinical psychology, the natural limitations of various classification systems, and the limitations of our working memory – all influence how we conceptualize psychopathology and treat our patients in psychotherapy. Ibrahim Goksin Baser Clinical psychologist based in Istanbul, Turkey, and holds a doctoral degree in clinical psychology from both Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakif University and Istanbul Medeniyet University. His doctoral research focuses on exploring the interplay between emotional regulation difficulties, defensive styles, and dark triad personality traits. During his master’s studies, he received comprehensive training in systemically oriented family and couple therapy, narrative therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy. His academic pursuits took a turn towards affective neuroscience and neuropsychoanalysis after encountering the work of Jaak Panksepp. Ibrahim Goksin Baser also maintains a private practice as a psychotherapist. His professional journey reflects a commitment to both academic research and practical application within the field of clinical psychology. Sofia Kontaxi Ph.D. candidate and scientific researcher in the Department of General and Neurocognitive Psychology at the International Psychoanalytic University Berlin. She holds an M.A. in Clinical Psychology and has an extensive background in EEG research, with prior work focusing on attention and conflict processing in patients with panic disorder and depression, as well as emotional processing. Her current research bridges neuropsychoanalysis, cognitive neuroscience, personality, examining individual differences in motivational and affective processing based on Panksepp's primary affective systems. With a foundation in psychoanalytic theory, she is pursuing a long-term goal of integrating clinical practice and research through psychotherapist training. She is particularly interested in how neurocognitive methods can illuminate psychoanalytic questions and how insights gained from the exploration of cognitive processes in neuroscience can be integrated into psychoanalytic practice to enhance the understanding of the human mind. Saul Rosenberg Psychoanalyst and psychologist with extensive experience in the clinical and forensic assessment and psychoanalytic treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder. His recent book chapter, “Forensic Assessment of Psychological Injury Claims,” provides a critical review of the current state of science in assessing PTSD within litigation contexts. (Young et al. Eds. 2025. Handbook of Psychological Injury and Law, Springer). Dr. Rosenberg was a member of Robert Wallerstein's research group which developed structured clinical interviews and rating scales for measuring therapeutic change in psychoanalytic treatment (DeWitt, K. N., Hartley, D. E., Rosenberg, S. E., Zilberg, N. J., & Wallerstein, R. S. 1991. Scales of psychological capacities: Development of an assessment approach, Psychoanalysis and Contemporary Thought, 14(2), 343-361). Alicia Golijov Psychotherapist and Psychoanalyst who specializes in neurorehabilitation and neurocognitive stimulation – MA NRH – E NC. She is the founder and coordinator of AINPSA, the director and psychotherapist of MOEBIUS: psychology, body, and communication, a member of SEN and NPSA, and a teacher and workshop lead for emotional management groups. Alla Landa Associate Professor of Clinical Psychology in Psychiatry and PI of the Developmental Psychosomatics Laboratory at Columbia University Medical Center in New York. She is a clinical psychologist trained in developmental neuroscience, who specializes in multidisciplinary research and treatment of psychosomatic distress. Bridging clinical psychology, psychoanalysis and neuroscience, her work is focused on the interface of emotion regulation, interpersonal well-being, lifespan development, and bodily health, with the goal of uncovering etiology of psychosomatic distress and developing new, effective treatments for these conditions as well as alleviating distress of medical illness. In particular, she has formulated a translational research-based Developmental Theory of Centralized/Somatoform Pain and its implications for treatment. Both researcher and clinician, she also conducts comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluations, as well as psychotherapy in private practice. Dr. Landa is also the founder and director of the Columbia Psychosomatics Conferences that have been engaging multidisciplinary group of researchers and clinicians from around the world and a novel Multidisciplinary Comprehensive Psychosomatics Training Program at CUMC. Andrea Clarici Psychoanalytic psychotherapist and psychiatrist from Trieste (Italy), working clinically in private psychoanalytic practice. He is also a professor in the course “Advanced Dynamic Psychology” at the Faculty of Psychology and the course “Child Neuropsychiatry” at the Faculty of Medicine, both at the University of Trieste (UNITS, Italy). He trained at the Centro Studi di Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica e Metodologia Istituzionale in Milan with psychoanalysts supervised and inspired by Joseph Sandler (IPA President 1989–1993) and his wife, Ann Marie Sandler. Andrea Clarici is coordinator of the training for psychoanalytic psychotherapy of the Centro di Formazione e Ricerca in Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica (CFR) in Trieste. He has worked psychoanalytically with brain-lesioned patients, on individual and group psychoanalytic psychotherapy for patients with neurofunctional (conversion) disorders at the Neurological Clinic of Trieste, and currently in psychotherapeutic support of oncological patients. He is on the staff of the Society of Neuropsychoanalysis as International Liaison Officer. In his effort to enhance this important interdisciplinary approach, he translated in Italian The Archeology of Mind by Jaak Panksepp and Lucy Biven, Clinical Studies in Neuropsychoanalysis by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms, and The Brain and the Inner World by Mark Solms and Oliver Turnbull. In 2018, he edited a collection of selected works of Mark Solms, ranging from 1997 to 2017, in a book with the title “La coscienza dell’Es” [The Conscious Id], all these books for Raffaello Cortina Publisher (Milan). In 2024, he also translated The Hidden Spring by Mark Solms[La fonte nascosta, in Italian] for Adelphi editore (Milan). Tom Tomaszewski UKCP-accredited psychoanalytic psychotherapist and EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing) Consultant working in private practice in Oxford and London, England. He completed a Master’s degree in Clinical Science at the University of Kent and his psychoanalytic training at the Canterbury Consortium of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapists. He served for three years as an honorary psychotherapist at St Martin’s Hospital in Canterbury, working with individuals experiencing psychosis, often seeing them in their own homes. He spent nearly ten years at Mandy Saligari’s clinic, Charter, a specialist and progressive addiction service, where he was clinical manager and senior clinician. As a group psychotherapist, he has also worked extensively with couples and families. He specializes in supporting individuals struggling with addiction, dependency, and the effects of oppression. He has published two novels (The Wisdom of Uncle Kasimir, Bloomsbury, 2006 and The Eleventh Letter, Dodo Ink, 2016), and wrote book reviews and features for the now defunct Independent on Sunday. A companion piece to this talk is a paper recently accepted for publication in the British Journal of Psychotherapy: “Be somebody else: improvisation, momentum, and psychoanalysis as social psychotherapy.” Aideen Nunan Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She received her psychoanalytic training at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis (NPAP) where she has served as Director of the Theodore Reik Consultation Center and as a Board Member, in addition to teaching and supervising students. She is a founding member of the Edith Laufer Neuropsychoanalytic Clinical Study Center of NPAP and serves as the Secretary of its Steering Committee. Ann Rose Simon Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and Westchester, NY who works with adults and children in individual, couple and family therapy. Ann Rose has completed psychoanalytic training NPAP, ORI and at the Anni Bergman Parent-infant Training Program, working with parents-infant dyads since 2012. She has been the Director of the Edith Laufer Neuropsychoanalytic Clinical Study Center of NPAP since 2022 and is currently the Co-Director. She was a founding member of the Center in 2003 and has maintained 3 or 4 brain-injured patients in her practice since 2003. In addition, she is the Coordinator of a Neuropsychoanalytic Reading/Study Group at NPAP and facilitates many of the discussions. She has presented clinical papers at the International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress in South Africa, Puerto Rico and New York. Robert Irwin Wolf Senior member and training analyst at the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis. He received his doctorate in Psychoanalytic Studies at the Parkmore Institute. He is both a licensed creative art therapist and a psychoanalyst in New York City where he has conducted a private Practice since 1975. He has published a series of articles and book chapters that have become part of the central pioneering literature on phototherapy. This presentation today will draw from his most recent article: “Synthesis of photography, art and neuropsychological concepts within psychoanalytic psychotherapy: an illustrated case study,” published in the British Journal of Psychotherapy, January 2024. Dr. Wolf was promoted to Professor Emeritus at the College of New Rochelle after teaching graduate art therapy students for 39 years. He held the position of Director of the Institute for Expressive. Analysis in New York City for three terms and was a past president of the New York Art Therapy Association. His training, teaching and clinical experience in 45 + years of private practice, has enabled him to integrate these experiences in uniquely clinical methods. As a fine art photographer, his photographs have won awards and have been published internationally. Mary Edlow Holds a master’s degree from Columbia University and a PhD from New York University. She earned a certificate in psychoanalysis from the National Association for Psychoanalysis (NPAP) where she has been an active member of the Edith Laufer Neuropsychoanalytic Clinical Study Center (ELNCSC) for the past 25 years. Dr. Edlow is currently a Co-Director of the ELNCSC, on the editorial board of NPAP’s journal, The Psychoanalyic Review, a member of the Curriculum Committee, and a permanent faculty member. Dr. Edlow is a longstanding member of The International Neuropsychoanalysis Society (NPSA), where she is a Clinical Fellow. She has contributed two papers to the society’s journal, Neuropsychoanalysis: Edlow, M. & Kahn, C. (2023). Reparative adaptation after brain injury facilitated by psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Neuropsychoanalysis, 25:1, 53-66, DOI:10.1080/15294145.2023.2196998 and Edlow, M. (2014). Injured brain, injured self: psychodynamic treatment of a patient with epilepsy. Neuropsychoanalysis, 16(2), 139–147. https://doi.org/10.1080/15294145.2014.963827. Dori Rubinstein Clinical psychologist, trauma specialist, and researcher with extensive experience working with trauma survivor populations. He holds a Ph.D. in Public Health with a specialization in Emergency Medicine from Ben-Gurion University. From 2020 to 2024, Dr. Rubinstein led the clinical development and research department at the Community Stress Prevention Center in Israel, where he also advised the Israeli Ministry of Health during wartime. Currently, Dr. Rubinstein is a Postdoctoral Associate at the Harpaz-Rotem PTSD Treatment & Research Lab in the Department of Psychiatry at Yale University School of Medicine. His research and practice focus on improving psychotherapy approaches, understanding the role of imagination, and enhancing resilience in trauma-exposed populations. Ilan Harpaz-Rotem Clinical psychologist and Professor of Psychiatry and Psychology at Yale University and a clinical psychologist specializing in trauma-related disorders. He serves as the Director of the PTSD Advanced Fellowship in Mental Illness Research and Treatment and as Deputy Director of the Evaluation Division at the National Center for PTSD, VA Connecticut Healthcare System. Dr. Harpaz-Rotem’s research focuses on improving treatments for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) by exploring neurobiological, psychological, and systemic factors influencing trauma response. His work includes studies on decision-making under risk, fear learning, and the integration of pharmacological agents like ketamine with psychotherapy. David Bullard Clinical psychologist and Clinical Professor– volunteer– in the departments of Medicine and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences, and is Consultant, Division of Palliative Medicine, University of California, San Francisco. He is a former Mentor, Center for Psychedelic Therapies & Research, California Institute of Integral Studies, and was awarded the 2023 Distinguished Contribution to Psychology Award by the California Psychological Association. Dr. Bullard consulted for many years with psychoanalyst Hal Sampson, PhD and has been a long-time member of the San Francisco Psychotherapy Research Group. His trauma-informed therapy background over the past 30 years includes EMDR and Somatic Experiencing, and he has been teaching an adaptation of the Flash Technique for the past 7 years. Dr. Bullard hosted two UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences’ seminars on the new paradigm of non-exposure trauma therapy: https://youtu.be/QGD4YSh-pMc and https://youtu.be/LX-07Xi2yJ0. Paul Siegel Clinical psychologist, Professor of Psychology at Purchase College, State University of New York (SUNY), and Research Professor of Psychiatry at the Keck School or Medicine, University of Southern California. His research focuses on unconscious emotional processes and their influence on behavior, particularly in the context of anxiety disorders. Dr. Siegel is renowned for developing the Very Brief Exposure (VBE) technique, which involves subliminal exposure to phobic stimuli to reduce fear responses without conscious awareness. His work has been supported by grants from the National Institute of Mental Health and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation. He has published extensively in peer-reviewed psychology and psychiatry journals, contributing to the understanding of unconscious emotion and its applications in clinical psychology. Richard D. Lane Professor of Psychiatry, Psychology, and Neuroscience at the University of Arizona. As a clinical psychiatrist and psychodynamic psychotherapist, he holds a PhD in Experimental Psychology, with a focus on systems neuroscience and emotion research. Dr. Lane was among the pioneers in conducting functional brain imaging studies of emotion in the 1990s and continues to explore emotion, emotional awareness, and neurovisceral integration using functional MRI. His research delves into the interplay between emotion, the brain, and heart disease, supported by various grants, including several RO1 awards from the NIH. Dr. Lane has authored over 200 papers and book chapters and is the senior editor of two books. He served as the director of the psychotherapy curriculum for psychiatric residents at the University of Arizona for more than two decades and has received multiple awards for teaching and mentoring. Dr. Lane’s work emphasizes integrating systems neuroscience with psychological concepts and bridging basic science with clinical applications. His research interests include emotional awareness, alexithymia, the role of emotion in mind–body interactions – such as susceptibility to sudden cardiac death – and the mechanisms by which memory and emotion interact to facilitate enduring change in psychotherapy. These themes are explored in the book Neuroscience of Enduring Change: Implications for Psychotherapy, published by Oxford University Press in 2020, which he co-edited with Lynn Nadel. In recognition of his contributions, Dr. Lane was named the Fulbright-Freud Visiting Lecturer in Psychoanalysis in 2023, hosted by the Sigmund Freud Museum in Vienna, Austria. He also received the Distinguished Scientist Award from the American Psychosomatic Society in 2024. Andrea C. Valente Contract Lecturer at the Faculty of Education, York University, Canada, teaching various undergraduate courses in philosophy and psychology of education, curriculum studies, educational linguistics, and research methodology. Dr. Valente’s doctoral, masters’, and specializations in Brazil, Canada, Germany, and Sweden enabled her to pursue interdisciplinary research across various fields of the humanities and social sciences. Currently, her research lies in neuropsychoanalysis, AI technology and discourse, and curriculum studies. She has collaborated with local and international scholars in diverse roles such as journal co-editor, writer, peer reviewer, and supervisor, among others. Dr. Valente is a mindfulness and yoga practitioner with a private practice. Richard Glisker Clinical psychologist and a current psychoanalytic candidate at the Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research. His doctoral research focused on schizotypy, attachment, and social cognition. Evert Boonstra Background in cognitive neuroscience and philosophy. He holds a PhD from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (The Netherlands). His work spans experimental and computational neuroscience, as well as the interfaces between Hegelian philosophy, neuroscience, and psychoanalysis. Currently, he is conducting a postdoctoral fellowship with Professor Mark Solms at the University of Cape Town. Susan P. Sherkow Training and Supervising Analyst at BPI, a Supervising Child and Adolescent Analyst at NYPSI, and on the faculties of Mt. Sinai and Albert Einstein College of Medicine. Founder of the not-for – profit Sherkow Center for Child Development and Autism Spectrum Disorder, she has presented and published extensively on the application of psychoanalytic developmental theory to the treatment of children, adolescents and adults with ASD, including a TEDx Talk and co-authorship of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Perspectives from Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience. Here follow the abstracts from the symposia and oral presentations that were selected for the Congress following a call for papers. Oliver Turnbull

Additional authors: Jade Witten, PhD; Emma Truss, MSc; Rudi Coetzer, PhD

Rage at strangers: Anger elicitation and regulation as a function of relationship type

Autobiographical recall is a powerful method for eliciting emotion, and plays a central role in the analytic process. However, the variable of relationship type has never been systematically studied in emotion elicitation – though of course relationship type is a key psychoanalytic variable. The present study investigated the effectiveness of an emotion memory task (Affective Story Recall) for anger elicitation, using five relationship categories (family, partner, friend, stranger, abstract). The study also investigated the effectiveness of two emotion regulation techniques (reappraisal and distraction) for anger modulation. 52 neurologically healthy adults completed a series of anger elicitation and regulation tasks, several neuropsychological measures of cognitive ability, and questionnaires on attachment style and the use of ER techniques. Most relationship categories selectively elicited anger, with some categories (especially Stranger) eliciting especially high levels. Both reappraisal and distraction reduced anger intensity across all relationship categories, except Stranger, where distraction was more effective. Distraction effectiveness was significantly predicted by three factors: the regular use of an ER technique, attachment style, and age. Cognitive control factors played no significant role. These findings have important applications for rehabilitation (allowing clinicians to tailor interventions to patients’ strengths and weaknesses), and of course also have implications for psychoanalysis. A paper based on this work was recently published: Witten, J.A., Truss, E., Coetzer, R. & Turnbull, O.H. (2023). Rage at Strangers: Anger elicitation and regulation as a function of relationship type. American Journal of Psychology. 136 (3): 273-289.

Kerry Kelly Novick  

Interdisciplinary, two systems, developmental, separateness, therapeutic alliance, transformation

In this commentary, the authors underscore Singletary and Rice's integrative, interdisciplinary approach to describing the role of love in intensive treatment of severe pathology. Novick and Novick bring to bear the psychoanalytic tradition of a dual-track model of development and apply their two-systems model of self-regulation to support the findings of the target paper authors. They elaborate on the idea of children as active agents of their solutions to the challenge of traumatic experience and apply their two-systems ideas, combined with those of the target paper, to suggest that an interdisciplinary approach can generate enhanced clinical techniques and amend psychoanalytic models of development and pathogenesis.

The Neuropsychoanalysis of Dreams: A Meta-Review Focusing on Neuroanatomy

Jette Borawski , Annakarina Mundorf , Sebastian Ocklenburg and Lena Barth

Lena Barth

Am Kaiserkai 1, Hamburg 20457, Germany
jette.borawski@medicalschool-hamburg.de

Hamburg, Germany

Hamburg, Germany

Bochum, Germany

Hamburg, Germany

Lena Barth  

Dreaming, dreams, meta-review, neuropsychoanalysis, psychoanalysis

For a long time, dreams were regarded as random mysterious constructs and psychoanalytical dream theories were often criticized due to lack of evidence. However, with the development of advanced neuroscientific techniques, increasing evidence has been found that dreams have underlying physiological correlates. Furthermore, dreams and their therapeutic application provide meaningful insights into the psychological experience of patients. This meta-review compares brain activation of human dreams by contrasting the Activation-Synthesis Model with a psychoanalytic perspective on dreams. Therefore, 22 review articles were examined, based on a systematic research strategy following PRISMA guidelines, and underwent a Risk of Bias assessment. The results emphasize neuroscientific evidence for the psychoanalytic model of dreams. In particular, an increased activation of the limbic system and prefrontal cortex was found indicating the emotional and memory-related content during the process of dreaming. Despite the strong tendency towards the psychoanalytical dream model, a few findings also provide suggestions for a revised Activation-Synthesis Model, which could be examined in future research. This paper aims to encourage expanding research in neuropsychoanalysis to integrate dreams more in psychotherapeutic interventions.

Hessel Boerboom  

The 23rd Annual Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society held in 2024 in Trieste, Italy, had as its theme the question: “How do subjective experiences become bodily disorders?” This is seen in conversion disorder (previously called “hysteria,” now called functional neurological disorder, or FND). The body “speaks,” but the speaker is not aware of its meaning. In that year, I reviewed a book by Jean Benjamin Stora on the theme of psychosomatics (Boerboom, 2024). The focus of that book was on the French school of psychosomatics, whereas in this new title by Schultz-Venrath we encounter the modern German school. His approach is based on the mentalization model, as introduced by Bateman and Fonagy. This is a complex theme, one at the heart of our field: neuropsychoanalysis. Additionally, it is the start of psychoanalysis, as the case of Anna O (who was diagnosed with hysteria) was for Freud an important source of inspiration. The way the mind influences the body has kept troubling psychoanalysis. In the six chapters of Schultz-Venrath’s book, we are not only introduced to this complex theme but also get a theoretical foundation for the advice Schultz-Venrath gives on therapy for these patients.

The first chapter introduces the concept of “mentalizing,” a term initially coined by Marty regarding preconscious processes, and more recently used by Fonagy, who conceptualizes mentalizing as a process involved in the development of the brain to infer the mental state of self and others. Schultz-Venrath summarizes the theories on the development of the brain in relation to the development of the affective self. The mentalization model he uses in this book rests on the theory of the formation of representations of affects. It tries to integrate findings by Stern, Damasio, Panksepp, Leikert, and Solms. Schultz-Venrath notes that there is no consensus as to what exactly affects, emotions, and feelings are, and how the self arises from them. He concludes that Panksepp’s affective neuroscience seems the best model to answer those questions. The development of a mentalizing self starts in the womb. For the newborn, affective touch is essential; and in further development, attachment, the relation to the primary caregiver - and later on others - plays a vital role. Representations are formed in the mind as “memories” of bodily encounters and bodily reactions. Marty developed his concept of mentalizing in reaction to Alexander’s specificity model. He saw somatization as a failure of mentalization. The French (and German) model of mentalization was (and is) used to understand psychosomatic disorders, whereas in the Anglo-Saxon world, mentalization is used as part of the treatment of borderline personality disorders. In this “culture,” the relationship between attachment and mentalization is further developed without much regard for the psychosomatic associations because the authors use the same word for different meanings.

Philadelphia, United States

Jane Abrams  

Child therapy, neurodivergent, interdisciplinary, subjectivity, attachment

In her article, “A subjectivity of one's own: Neuropsychological differences and the shaping of experience” (2025), Dr. Christina Peters demonstrates how psychoanalytic and neurobiological perspectives can converge to deepen our understanding of the interpersonal challenges and developmental risks for neurodivergent children. Peters describes her treatment of 7-year -old Gwen, illustrating how her difficulties with motor planning and language processing interfered with her parents' ability to meet her needs, resulting in shared feelings of failure, frustration and shame. Peters formed an interdisciplinary team comprised of an OT, a speech and language therapist, and Gwen's parents. Together they identified the nature of Gwen's processing differences and developed interventions that made attuned and reciprocal communication possible. Peters contributed her psychoanalytic knowledge to the team's understanding of Gwen. However, she emphasizes the critical importance of expanding psychoanalytic approaches to include neuroscientific perspectives.

48th Bulletin of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society

Several members from regional groups participated in the recent Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society held in New York City in June, 2025, highlighting the enthusiasm and significant work each group is undertaking within their respective regions to promote and advance knowledge in neuropsychoanalysis. Our regional groups continue to hold frequent meetings that include presentations, discussions, clinical case supervisions, and critical analyses of articles published in our journal. Webinars are organized to address specific topics, either with the support of the Society or independently. Notable speakers have included Douglas Watt, Maggie Zellner, Tamara Fischmann, and Mark Solms.

An exciting theme across the regional group reports in this issue is the expansion of multidisciplinary collaboration in neuropsychoanalysis. Our groups have made substantial contributions to the dissemination of neuropsychoanalysis by integrating members from diverse professional backgrounds, including psychotherapists, neuroscientists, neurologists, healthcare professionals working in various settings, and even dance artists. This bulletin, which reports the activities of eleven groups, reflects their experiences and significant achievements, such as the publication of articles and the writing and translating of books. The primary topics addressed in these publications include affective neuroscience, free energy, predictive coding, and studies on the unconscious, thereby enriching the dialogue between psychoanalysis and neuroscience. Furthermore, the regional groups extend invitations for new members to join and encourage collaborations among groups with the goal of fostering continued growth within this vibrant neuropsychoanalytic community.

Ana Delgadillo Hernández

Jane Abrams

Neuropsychoanalysis Group of Vienna, Austria

The composition of the Vienna Neuropsychoanalysis group, as mentioned in the previous bulletin, has changed in that regular meetings in the former constellation are no longer taking place. In recent years, Mark Solms has conducted seminars on neuropsychoanalysis at the Vienna Psychoanalytic Academy, a center for psychoanalysis and its applications, jointly established by the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society and the Vienna Psychoanalytic Association. Since 2024, he has also offered four semester-long seminars entitled “Clinical Work with Concepts by Mark Solms,” focusing on key psychoanalytic concepts in the light of neuroscientific findings.

Body and Self in Functional Neurological Disorders**

Selma Aybek and Olaf Blanke

Olaf Blanke

Pr Selma Aybek, Rue du musée 5, 1700 Fribourg, Switzerland
selma.aybek@unifr.ch

Geneva, Switzerland

Geneva, Switzerland

Olaf Blanke  

Functional neurological disorder, conversion disorder, neuropsychoanalysis, conversion disorder, bodily self

In this commentary, we comment on the closing remarks from Mark Solms at the 2024 International Neuropsychoanalysis conference in light of recent developments in neurosciences around functional neurological disorders (FND). FND is the new term used to designate a frequent medical condition, which has seen several paradigm shifts over the last century; previously considered a diagnosis of exclusion (made when no other neurological disease was found), it is now a rule-in process, a positive diagnosis based on clinical examination. The pathophysiology of FND is now understood in the framework of clinical neurosciences with underlying mechanisms such as abnormal emotional processing, predictive coding and multisensory integration of interoceptive signals and other bodily signals. Neuroscience and neuropsychoanalysis are two important converging fields toward better understanding of the condition and better care for patients.

Mind / Body Metaphors and Predictive Coding Commentary on Mark Solms’ Target Article – “Function” in Functional Neurological Disorders: The Common Ground of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis

Iftah Biran

Iftah Biran

6 Weizmann st. Tel Aviv, 6423906, Israel
i_biran@hotmail.com

Iftah Biran  

Solms examines the mind–body problem, particularly the hard problem of consciousness, from two perspectives that appear contrasting at first glance. The first is the classic mind–body problem: how subjective experiences (i.e. qualia, consciousness) emerge from biological systems. The second, which reverses the classic problem, explores how the psyche influences the body – particularly in cases of hysteria (conversion or functional neurological disorders), where, as Solms states, “something mental can become something physical” (p. 3) implying the transformation from the psyche to the body.

Solms discusses two metaphors/analogies that shed light on the first aspect of the problem, both of which are drawn from Freud.

The first, Freud’s poem-alphabet metaphor, captures the idea that sensory and motor inputs are not simply copied into the brain in a fixed manner. Instead, they are transformed, restructured, and imbued with meaning – just as letters are arranged into words, sentences, and, ultimately, poetry. In a poem, the alphabet is not simply listed in order; rather, its elements are woven into a complex structure that conveys emotion, meaning, and intention. This metaphor highlights the creative, constructive nature of brain function: just as a poem gives new meaning to individual letters through their arrangement and interaction, the brain organises raw neural inputs into meaningful experiences, thoughts, and actions.

The second metaphor is the telescope-microscope analogy. Freud uses this analogy to describe the structure and function of the mind. He compares the mental apparatus to optical instruments that process images through multiple intermediate stages before producing a final image. Just as a telescope or microscope does not contain the image itself within its physical components but instead creates it through a sequence of lenses and adjustments, the mind is structured as a system where psychical processes occur at different functional levels rather than being tied to specific anatomical locations or neuronal substrates. Just as different points within an optical system contribute to the formation of an image without any one point being the sole “location” of the image, thoughts, memories, and perceptions arise from distributed, dynamic interactions within the brain. Freud uses this analogy to argue that the mind should not be understood anatomically, but rather functionally, as a system where different layers of processing contribute to consciousness and cognition.

Mark Edwards

Mark Edwards

London SE5 8AB, UK
mark.j.edwards@kcl.ac.uk

Mark Edwards  

Conversion disorder, predictive processing, functional neurological disorder, Freud

This commentary discusses Solms’s recent paper on the application of predictive processing theory to understand functional neurological disorder, and to put in context work by Freud and others that has previously sought to provide an explanatory framework for this condition. The commentary addresses the way in which predictive processing can become a unifying mechanism to link previous pathophysiological accounts and to arrive at a more general theoretical understanding of these disorders, and to provide pragmatic direction for clinical and research work.

History and Pathophysiology of Functional Neurological Disorders**

Richard Lane

Richard Lane

2800 E. Ajo Way, Tucson, AZ 85713-6204, USA
lane@email.arizona.edu
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-4074-1407

Richard Lane  

Functional neurological disorders, emotion, affective agnosia, predictive processing, allostasis

Thanks to Freud’s seminal insight we know that the idea of the body, not known neurological pathways, is the basis for functional neurological disorders (FND). Whereas Freud proposed that the functional impairment in these disorders had symbolic significance, this commentary focuses on three main ideas that are consistent with Freud’s insight but explain the mechanism of FNDs somewhat differently: (1) FNDs may arise from a deficit or failure in mental representation of emotion as opposed to defenses such as repression; (2) rather than having symbolic significance, bodily symptoms and signs often lack it, consistent with a failure in mental representation; (3) rather than the primary source of distress being an unmet need creating a deviation from a homeostatic set point that is resolved in a bottom-up manner, a complementary perspective is that bodily symptoms arise due to allostasis, a prediction of what is needed in the moment in interaction with the environment, that gets transmitted to the body in a top-down manner. These proposed mechanisms have implications for clinical interventions that could be of benefit to some patients.

Commentary on Solms’ “‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders”: On the Essence of Freud’s Theory

Michael Michael

Michael Michael

50 Yonsei-ro, Seodaemun-gu, Seoul, South Korea
mmichael.esq@gmail.com

Michael Michael  

Freud’s theory of hysteria, FND, predictive coding, Bayesian account, mind–body problem, repression

In his paper, Mark Solms highlights Freud’s profound neuroscientific insights as they relate to functional neurological disorders (FND). These include Freud’s view of hysteria as a disorder at the level of ideas and his related emphasis on the importance of function in our comprehension of the mind, his understanding of hierarchical processing, and his recognition that these processes are based on fundamental biological needs, as captured in his concepts of drives and energy. While I endorse these interpretations and their illumination of Freud as a foresighted neuroscientific thinker, I question the extent to which they are specific to psychoanalysis. Instead, I argue that Freud’s distinctively psychoanalytic contribution to the theory of hysteria lies in his emphasis on repression. Thus, while modern Bayesian approaches to FND vindicate much of Freud’s neuroscientific understanding of the disorder, they do not yet incorporate its specifically psychoanalytic dimension – something that would require assigning a central role to repression in the process.

Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

College Road, Bangor, Wales, LL57 2DG, UK
o.turnbull@bangor.ac.uk

Oliver Turnbull  

Functional neurological disorders, neurology, psychiatry

Prof. Solms makes several useful points around our understanding of functional neurological disorders. This commentary discusses three of these issues. First, the question of how this is a phenomenon rebranded, having long existed under different names. Second, the matter of how to treat our patients, where there are many advantages in not re-referring them, and in taking a pragmatic approach to their treatment. Finally, there is the interesting issue of whether, and if so how, functional neurological disorders might be regarded as the mind–body problem “in reverse.”

ARTICLE HISTORY Received 19 May 2025; Accepted 26 May 2025

We devote this issue to a fascinating topic that was closely involved with the creation of psychoanalysis, namely, that of hysteria, later called conversion disorder, and currently named functional neurological symptom disorder (FND). We present an updated discussion on the topic that encompasses diverse perspectives including the neurological, the psychiatric and neuropsychiatric, the psychoanalytic, and the neuropsychoanalytic. This issue publishes a brilliant target article by Mark Solms, “‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders: The Common Ground of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis” (Solms, 2025). Based on Solms’ closing remarks at the 23rd Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society held in Trieste, Italy in 2024, the paper goes back to the neuroanatomical background of Freud’s early career to show how hysterical symptoms became one of his main interests to the degree that made him abandon his neurological work and attempt to explain the way the mind works. Fourteen authors wrote commentaries that discuss Solms’ proposal. The authors come from different backgrounds that elaborate on the advances of an intriguing topic still in search of answers. Jon Stone’s commentary titled “The Legacy of Psychoanalysis for Functional Neurological Disorder (FND): Insights and Harms” addresses the importance of giving a place to FND in neurology as well as in psychoanalysis (Stone, 2025). He discusses his preference for the name FND instead of conversion disorder, arguing that the disorder is multifactorial. Mark Edwards’ commentary is entitled “How to Lesion an Idea – Commentary on Solms: ‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders” and it describes FND symptoms as a consequence of consciousness. He considers Freud’s ideas on hysteria important contributions and addresses the question on how an idea can be lesioned (Edwards, 2025). Selma Aybek and Olaf Blanke present a commentary titled “Body and Self in Functional Neurological Disorders” that highlights that FND is not a diagnosis of exclusion anymore, and that it has become a positive diagnosis based on clinical examination. They propose that the sense of agency might be an aspect to encourage collaborative work of psychoanalysis and neuroscience (Aybek & Blanke, 2025). Gerald Wiest contributed another commentary by the title “Functional neurological disorders: from the reflex arc model to the predictive mind” in which he underscores the application of the predictive coding model to understand somatoform symptoms and FND. He discusses the role of attention in FND symptoms and states that the predictive coding theory keeps room for the unconscious symbolic hypothesis of psychoanalysis (Wiest, 2025). Michael T. Michael’s “Commentary on Solms’ “‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders”: On the Essence of Freud’s Theory” emphasized that Freud’s knowledge of neuroscience and philosophy was remarkable, and that many of his ideas had been advanced by other authors before him. In his opinion, Solms’ perspective should give more importance to the essence of Freudian psychoanalysis, namely, repression, which would be the cause of hysterical symptoms for Freud (Michael, 2025). Oliver Turnbull’s commentary is titled “Functional Neurological Disorders: A Century of Passing the Buck” and it discusses that FND is an uncomfortable disorder for neurology, which has led to its different names. Priors: Multiple Memories or Parallel Processing? A Commentary on Mark Solms’ Original Lecture and the Ensuing Target Article “‘Function’ in Functional Neurological Disorders: The Common Ground of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis”

Marco Onofrj and Davide Liviello

Davide Liviello

via Polacchi 39, 66100, Chieti, Italy
onofrj@unich.it

Chieti, Italy

Davide Liviello  

Eels, functional neurologic disorders, priors, default mode network, frontal lobe

This short commentary on Solms highlights three points in his paper. The first is Freud’s intuition of the lifecycle of eels, showing that his prodigious mind was blooming, even when he was assigned a perfunctory task as a young biology researcher. The second is the concept that the body periphery is no longer contained topologically in the higher parts of the brain, but only functionally. Our commentary shows that functional outcomes of movements, instead of topological maps of body muscles, are automatically recruited by the basal ganglia motor circuits. The third is a short discussion of priors, parallel processing and emotional brain, by comparing Solms’ conceptions with ideas and terms used by authors working in the neuroscience or neuroethics fields.

Commentary on “Function” in Functional Neurological Disorders: The Common Ground of Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis by Mark Solms

David Olds

David Olds

New York City, NY, USA
ddolds@msn.com

David Olds  

ARTICLE HISTORY Received 26 January 2025; Accepted 25 April 2025

In his Target Article, Solms (2025) makes the following point beautifully:

When Freud, as a neurologist, tried to discern the ontological substrate of language, he came to the conclusion that it was something functional rather than anatomical: something ‘virtual’ which exists not within the elements of the nervous system but between them. (p. 15; emphasis in the original)

Thus, the betweenness is a very important point and may be one of the major elements in the evolution from molecules to signs. Function is a complex term. When we use it, we are usually explaining how something works, and we may say the function of the heart is to pump blood. One thing noted in this discussion is that a function has a purpose. And the reason that that function keeps happening is for that purpose, which benefits the organism. One thing to make clear is that with a function there are at least two elements, simply put, the cause and the effect. And when we do the cause, it is usually to get the effect, and it usually works. But what does it mean to say “functional rather than anatomical”? An immediate thought might be that “anatomical” is about where and how something works, and functional may be more about why it is chosen and why it works. Thus, we focus on the purpose more than on the mechanism.

And with a functional disorder, that function is what we want to understand: how the patient uses it to solve an emotional, usually unconscious problem. Anatomically, that sequence of neurological events would never be used to solve a normal problem. With an upper arm paralysis, the arm may be paralyzed to avoid one of its functions, such as aggression. The interference will be in the mind, in the communication and transfer between affects, and less in the neurons. And the work of therapy will be to discover that purpose. As we go up the evolutionary ladder that Solms describes, at each level the apparatus becomes more and more complex, and there may be more than one possible function.

Mark Solms  

Functional neurological disorder, Freud, psychoanalysis, predictive processing

This is a series of replies to the commentaries, written in the order in which they were received. The replies are followed by four conclusions: (1) many people still confuse “function” with physiology; (2) those who adopt the predictive processing paradigm still prioritize cognition over affect; (3) we should not underestimate the lingering antipathy towards and mistrust of psychoanalysis among medical scientists; (4) the neurologists who attended our Trieste congress left it with an improved attitude toward and understanding of psychoanalysis.

Introduction

The two books that are the subjects of this review have a long history and deal with an important means of evolution for psychoanalysis. In the last decades of the 20th century, psychoanalysis came under pressure because of a growing number of types of psychotherapy, a growing discussion on key concepts of psychoanalysis, and a growing concern about its results in comparison with CBT and medication. Around the turn of the century, psychoanalytical organizations reacted. In a guest editorial in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis, Emde and Fonagy reported on the Research Training Program (RTP) that had started in 1995 and that has since continued in one form or the other. Emde and Fonagy conclude: “The extent of its contribution (i.e. the RTP) to an emerging culture of research for our field will become apparent in the years to come. Many of us believe that the vitality of psychoanalysis depends on such a culture” (Emde & Fonagy, 1997, p. 651).

The International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA) has organized various research platforms. One of them started in 2006, the yearly Sandler Research Conference. The European Psychoanalytic Federation (EPF) has also organized several Working Parties. They “arose from the recognition that to be recognized as a scientific discipline involved better communication between psychoanalysts about how they understand their work and the clinical observations in which it is grounded” (Levy et al., 2024, p. 2). And, of course, in the same vein, the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society (NPSA) was formed, also with yearly conferences, with their core being the meeting of the neurosciences and psychoanalysis.

Both the IPA and the EPF initiatives have resulted in many books. Look them up in the references, they all contain a lot of information, including the IPA-initiative of Fonagy et al. (2002), Leuzinger-Bohleber & Kächele (2015), Leuzinger-Bohleber et al. (2003), and Leuzinger-Bohleber et al. (2016, 2020, 2022) that reported on the results of the Sandler-conferences. The EPF-initiative was documented in Tuckett (2008) and recently in Levy et al. (2024).

In the Introduction to the book, Luca Possati describes his intention to develop a “new research method” that engages with the theoretical frameworks and methods of Freudian psychoanalysis. In his view, actor network theory (ANT), material engagement theory (MET) and “biosemiotics,” when considered together, lead to a new research method he calls “technoanalysis.” Technoanalysis shows how the bi-directional recursive movement of “unconscious dynamics influence and shape technology and how, in turn, technology influences and shapes the unconscious” (2023, p. 7).

Possati recognizes that the human capacity to absorb, understand and competently address the complex ethical implications and social impacts of rapid technological development falls well below the immense complexity of its accomplishments. This is no new insight, in that ancient and contemporary philosophers and theologians also warn of the disastrous potential consequences of unbridled technological developments. Mythic narratives such as those about Icarus or Prometheus illustrate the tragic consequences when technology is used to transgress the laws of nature. Trevor Hjertaas  

Luria, affect, emotion, working brain

Alexander Luria is considered by many to be the father of neuropsychology. Known to only a few, however, is the fact that Luria was also keenly aware of the emotional aspects of mental life, examining these in conjunction with neurocognitive functioning in a manner similar to what we currently think of as affective neuroscience or affective neuropsychology. Neuropsychoanalytic clinicians Oliver Turnbull and Christian Salas (and their colleagues Alfredo Ardila, Rashad Bagus, and Monica Rossilli) explore this little-known aspect of Luria's work in their article: “Separated at birth: Rediscovering the lost emotions in Luria's Working Brain.” This article is reviewed in the research digest, recounting the intellectual adventure of the re-discovery of the sections specific to emotion in Luria's most famous text (and the translated presentation of these recovered chapters in their entirety).

jon.stone@ed.ac.uk

Jon Stone  

Functional neurological disorder, conversion disorder, Freud, psychoanalysis, predictive processing

There are many important insights from psychoanalysis that continue to be valuable when thinking about functional neurological disorder (FND). There is also however a legacy of harm related to the implementation of psychoanalytic theory in FND over the last century. This includes the accentuation of a dualistic, purely psychological model; the replacement of nineteenth century multifactorial models with a superficially more simplistic view; and encouraging disbelief of patient’s own narrative accounts. Predictive processing models and a much larger scientific evidence base offer an opportunity to revisit and update psychoanalytic hierarchical accounts of FND while acknowledging past harms.
